title: Cat Food Company
question: Estimate the number of cat food packets sold in one year in India.
solution_approach:
Consulting Core Group 2026-2027
Estimate the number of cat food packets sold in one year in India.
Alright. Just a couple of clarifying questions before I begin. Are we talking about a
specific brand or cat food in general?
In general. You don’t need to focus on a brand.
Got it. I myself don’t have any pets, so I was wondering how much cat food does one
cat typically consume?
You can assume one packet lasts around two weeks.
Okay. Lastly, do I need to consider price or revenue?
Just estimate the number of packets sold. Focus on demand only.
In that case, I'll estimate household cats by moving from population → households →
pet-owning households → cat-owning households → number of cats per household.
India's population is roughly 1.4 billion. I'll split this into urban and rural populations,
assuming 30% urban and 70% rural. To keep the estimate manageable, I'd like to focus
primarily on urban India.
My reasoning is that while rural households may own cats, packaged cat food
penetration is likely much lower because pets are often fed household food or
leftovers. Since we're estimating commercial cat food demand, I expect urban India to
account for the majority. Would that be a reasonable assumption?
Thats’s reasonable. Please proceed.
So urban population = 0.3 × 1.4B = 420 million. Assuming an average family size of 4,
this translates to approximately 105 million urban households.
Before estimating pet ownership, I'd like to segment households by income, as pet
ownership and spending on packaged pet food are likely correlated with income
levels. I'll assume 20% upper class, 60% middle class and 20% lower class. That gives us
21 million upper-class households, 63 million middle-class households and 21 million
lower-class households. Do the numbers and assumptions seem reasonable?

5.25M × 30% = 1.575 million cat-owning households.

On the other hand, younger urban pet owners are increasingly adopting packaged

title: EV Copper Usage
question: Estimate the amount of copper used in electric vehicles in India.
solution_approach:
Consulting Core Group
Estimate the amount of copper used in electric vehicles in India
Sure. Before I begin, I'd like to clarify a few things to better define the scope of the
problem.
Go ahead.
First, should I consider all EVs sold in India, or only those manufactured domestically?
Focus only on vehicles manufactured in India
Understood. Second, should I include only the copper present within the vehicles
themselves, or also account for associated infrastructure such as charging stations
and grid upgrades?
Only the copper used within the vehicles.
Got it. Lastly, should I cover all major EV categories such as two-wheelers, three-
wheelers, passenger cars and buses?
Yes, include all major categories.
Perfect. To solve this, I'd first estimate the number of EVs manufactured across
different vehicle segments and then estimate the amount of copper used per vehicle.
Sounds reasonable. How would you break down the EV market?
I'd start by segmenting EV production into four major categories:
Two-wheelers
Three-wheelers
Passenger cars
Electric buses
These segments differ significantly in production volume and vehicle architecture, so I
believe they should be analyzed separately.
My initial thought is to identify the major systems where copper is used inside an EV.
These would include:
Battery pack
Electric motor
Wiring harnesses and cabling
Power electronics such as inverters and controllers
Charging-related electrical systems
Okay. How would you organize that information?
I would actually create a matrix.
The rows would represent vehicle categories and the columns would represent major
copper-consuming systems.
This allows me to estimate copper usage component by component for each vehicle
type while ensuring I don't miss any major source of consumption.
Fair. Once you've segmented the market, how would you
estimate copper usage?
Good. Why use a matrix instead of simply estimating copper per vehicle category?
There are two reasons.
First, different vehicle types allocate copper differently. For example, a bus may
have significantly more wiring and battery-related copper than a two-wheeler.
Second, breaking the estimate into components creates a more transparent
structure. If one assumption appears unrealistic, it can be adjusted
independently without affecting the entire framework.
EV Industry Copper Usage - Interview Transcript
Guesstimate | Transport | McKinsey & Co.
272026-2027
Consulting Core Group
Makes sense. How would you proceed after creating the matrix?
For every cell in the matrix, I would estimate average copper content.
For example:
Copper in the battery system of a passenger car
Copper in the motor of a passenger car
Copper in the wiring of a passenger car
and so on across all vehicle categories.
Adding these values would give me the total copper per vehicle for that segment.
And then?
Any other way you could structure this?
Then I'd estimate annual production volumes for each EV category.
For each segment:
Copper Used = Number of Vehicles Manufactured × Average Copper per Vehicle
I would repeat this calculation across all segments and aggregate the results to arrive
at total copper consumption.
An alternative approach would be to begin with copper-consuming components
rather than vehicle categories.
For example:
Battery systems
Motors
Wiring
Power electronics
Then estimate how many of each component are produced across the EV industry
and the copper required per component.
However, I prefer the vehicle-segmentation approach because production statistics
are generally reported by vehicle category, making the estimation process more
straightforward.
Yes. I would pay particular attention to buses and commercial vehicles.
Although they represent a much smaller share of production volume compared to
two-wheelers, their copper content per vehicle is substantially higher. Therefore, they
could contribute a disproportionately large share of total copper demand.
Good observation. Let's stop here.
That's a fair choice. Anything else you'd keep in mind?

title: Agrochemicals Market Sizing
question: Estimate the market size for agrochemicals in the Sangrur district of Punjab.
solution_approach:
Consulting Core Group
Sangrur is a district in Punjab, and I want you to estimate the market size for
agrochemicals in this district. You can ask me for any data you need along the way.
Before jumping in, I have a few preliminary questions to better understand the
context.
First, when you say "agrochemicals," do you mean just fertilisers and pesticides, or
should I also consider herbicides, insecticides, and other farm-related chemicals?
You can include all types of agrochemicals commonly used in agriculture.
Great. Also, do we know whether agriculture is the primary occupation in Sangrur?
Yes, you can assume that agriculture is the main livelihood there.
Alright. Do we know how these agrochemicals reach the district? Are they
manufactured locally or sourced from outside?
You can assume they are sourced from multiple external suppliers. So, the source is
not relevant for this case.
Got it. One final clarification, should I estimate the market size in terms of volume
(kg/litre) or revenue (Rupees)?
Let's go with revenue.
Understood. So, broadly speaking, my market size formula will be:
Market Size = Σ  (Cultivated Area by Crop) × (Agrochemical Usage per Unit Area) × (Price
per Unit of Agrochemical)
This would be calculated across each major crop and agrochemical type. Does that
approach work?
I'd like to understand the total cultivated land area in Sangrur. Do we have data on
what percentage of the district is under agriculture?
We don't have exact figures, but if you had to estimate it, how would you go about it?
Well, I'd begin with national averages. From what I recall, land in India is primarily used
for agriculture, commercial, and residential purposes. Among these, agriculture
typically dominates.
Yes, that sounds like a solid starting point. Where would you like to begin?
Correct. Agriculture is indeed the largest. Nationally, about 15% of the land is used for
agriculture. However, in a district like Sangrur, that percentage would be much higher.
Agrochemicals Market Sizing - Interview Transcript
Guesstimate | Agrochemicals  | McKinsey & Co.
33
Understood. Would it be reasonable to assume 30% for Sangrur?
Yes, you can go with that.
Do we know the total area of Sangrur?
Yes, it's around 4,000 square kilometres.
So, with 30% land under agriculture, that's 1,200 sq. km of cultivated area.
Next, could you share the crop-wise distribution in this district?
Sangrur is primarily divided between wheat and rice. You can assume 50% each for
simplicity.
Got it. That means 600 sq. km each for wheat and rice.
Would it be reasonable to further segment agrochemicals into different categories
and estimate the spend for each crop based on factors such as crop requirements,
farmer affordability, product availability, and adoption levels?
2026-2027
Consulting Core Group
That's a reasonable approach. But to keep the calculations manageable, let's use an
average agrochemical spend per crop.
Instead of going into individual agrochemicals, can I take an average agrochemical
spend per crop per unit area?
Yes, that's fine. For reference:
Wheat: ₹2,00,000 per sq. km
Rice: ₹1,00,000 per sq. km
This includes all agrochemicals.
Thanks. So
Total cultivated land = 1,200 sq. km
50% under wheat = 600 sq. km × ₹2,00,000 = ₹12 crore
50% under rice = 600 sq. km × ₹1,00,000 = ₹6 crore
So total market = ₹12 crore + ₹6 crore = ₹18 crore
Before finalising, I'd like to sanity-check the estimate from a farmer's perspective.
We estimated 1,200 sq. km of cultivated land, which translates to roughly 3 lakh acres.
At a market size of ₹18 crore, this implies an average annual agrochemical spend of
about ₹600 per acre. Assuming an average farmer in Punjab cultivates 4–6 acres, this
implies an annual expenditure of roughly ₹2,500–₹3,500 per farmer.
Given that fertilisers, pesticides, and other crop protection chemicals are essential
inputs applied multiple times during a cropping cycle, an annual spend of roughly
₹2,500–₹3,500 per farmer appears reasonable and affordable.
That's a good sanity check.
But, let's say the actual market size is only ₹10 crore. Why do you think your estimate
is off?
Agrochemicals Market Sizing - Interview Transcript
Guesstimate | Agrochemicals  | McKinsey & Co.
34
I'd systematically identify where my assumptions may have overestimated demand. I
would bucket the reasons into three categories:
Demand-side Factors (Farmers)
Adoption of sustainable or organic farming practices might be reducing
agrochemical usage.
Farmers are using lower quantities than assumed.
Price-sensitive farmers are opting for cheaper alternatives such as neem or cow
dung-based treatments.
Supply-side Factors (Company / Market)
The presence of counterfeit or unbranded agrochemical products reducing
branded market revenue.
Weak distribution network leading to lower penetration in smaller towns and
villages.
Stock-outs or poor retailer availability limiting sales.
External Factors
Weather conditions reducing the need for agrochemicals.
Crop rotation or changes in cropping patterns.
Government regulations or subsidy changes affecting agrochemical purchases.
That's a comprehensive set of reasons.
Assuming 80% of farmers use branded products and 20% use local alternatives at half
the cost, the market size reduction is driven by this shift to cheaper options. What
recommendations would you give to the company to address this?
2026-2027
Consulting Core Group
I would recommend the following initiatives:
Short-Term Recommendations
1.Strengthen the distribution network to improve product availability in rural
markets.
2.Launch farmer awareness campaigns demonstrating the effectiveness and long-
term benefits of branded agrochemicals.
3.Introduce smaller pack sizes or promotional pricing to make products more
affordable for price-sensitive farmers.
Long-Term Recommendations
1.Invest in R&D to develop cost-effective formulations without compromising
product quality.
2.Build stronger relationships with farmers through field demonstrations, training
sessions, and partnerships with agricultural cooperatives.
3.Continuously monitor competitor pricing and local market trends to remain
competitive while protecting margins.
Good. That makes sense. We can conclude the interview here.

well? Also, should I consider only domestic operations, or international operations
as well?
Let's keep it simple-focus only on domestic commercial passenger aircraft.

route due to frequency requirements, turnaround time, and maintenance
rotations?
Yes, that's a reasonable assumption.
Perfect. I'll approach this in three steps. First, estimate the number of domestic air

across airlines operating in India. Does that sound reasonable?
Go ahead.

metro cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kolkata, Ahmedabad,
and Pune.

connectivity: 8C2 = 28 routes
Then, each metro likely connects to smaller cities.
Assume each metro connects to ~7 tier-2 cities
→ ( 8 times 7 = 56 )
So total routes:
28 + 56 = 84
I'll round that to roughly 85 routes.
Makes sense so far. How do you go from routes to aircraft?
To estimate aircraft requirements, I'd like to start with a representative metro-to-
metro route. I'll work through one example route first - Delhi to Mumbai, a high-
frequency trunk route - then generalize.
Assume a one-way flight time of 2 hours and a turnaround time of 1 hour.
That gives a round-trip cycle time of:
2+1+2+1=6 hours
If an aircraft operates for roughly 12 hours a day, it can complete:
12/6=2 round-trip per day.
For a busy metro-to-metro route, I'll assume demand is roughly 8 round-trips per
day.
Therefore:
8/2=4 aircraft per metro route.
Generalizing across the network:
Delhi–Mumbai is an extreme case. Averaging across route types:
• Metro-to-metro (28 routes): ~4 aircraft per route
• Tier-2 routes (57 routes): lower frequency (~4 round trips/day), similar cycle time →
(6×4)÷12 = 2 aircraft

title: Bandra-Worli Sea Link
question: Estimate the annual revenue generated by the Bandra-Worli Sea Link toll collection.
solution_approach:
Consulting Core Group 2026-2027
Estimate the annual revenue generated by the Bandra-Worli Sea Link. The primary
source of revenue is toll collection from vehicles.
To estimate annual revenue, I’d like to begin by confirming: toll collection is the sole or
primary source of revenue, right?
Yes, the revenue is predominantly from toll charges.
Got it. Could you share more on toll operations? Specifically, how many toll lanes are
functional, and are they segregated by vehicle type?
There are three toll lanes in each direction, operational 24/7. All vehicle types use the
same lanes, no differentiation.
Understood. I'll also assume all six lanes run at full uptime year-round with no
significant maintenance closures, just to keep the estimate clean. Fair?
That's a fairly simplifying assumption.
Are the toll charges different for Light Motor Vehicles (LMVs) and Heavy Motor Vehicles
(HMVs)?
Yes. Assume LMVs pay ₹100, and you can use a reasonable assumption for HMVs.
I'll assume HMVs are charged ₹300, and I'll also assume a typical LMV:HMV ratio of
about 4:1. More cars and cabs through the day, more trucks at night. Does that work?
To estimate annual revenue, I'd like to break the problem into three parts:
1.Estimate the number of vehicles using the sea link on a typical day.
2.Split those vehicles by category, since different vehicle types pay different tolls.
3.Calculate daily revenue and annualize it while accounting for differences in traffic
across the year.
To estimate vehicle volume, I'll look at lane capacity, traffic intensity across different
times of the day, and any differences between weekdays and holidays.
Does that sound like a reasonable approach?
That's a reasonable assumption.
Yes, that’s a structured and logical approach.
Thanks. Since traffic isn't uniform across the day, I'd like to define three time
blocks: Peak hours from 7-11am and 4-8pm (8 hours total), Mid-peak from 11am-
4pm (5 hours), and Low-peak from 8pm-7am (11 hours). I'll estimate traffic using
occupancy levels relative to peak traffic. I'll assume mid-day traffic operates at
roughly 50% of peak capacity and night traffic at roughly one-sixth of peak
capacity, assuming mid-peak runs at about half of peak volume, and low-peak at
about one-sixth. Reasonable?
Bandra-Worli Sea Link - Interview Transcript
Guesstimate | Transport | McKinsey & Co.
40
Yes, you can proceed with that.
One operational question: should I assume all vehicles use FastTag, or do we need to
account for manual toll collection as well?
Yes, that's a fair way to model it.
One more consideration: given the bridge primarily serves commuter and
business traffic connecting the western suburbs to Nariman Point, would
weekday volumes be meaningfully higher than Sundays and public holidays?
Assume all vehicles use FastTag.
Next, since we're assuming uniform FastTag payments, can I assume each
vehicle clears the booth in roughly 20 seconds, with no manual-payment delays
to account for?
Consulting Core Group 2026-2027
In that case, would it be reasonable to treat Saturdays like regular weekdays, but
assume Sundays and public holidays, roughly 52 Sundays plus 25-30 holidays, so about
80 days a year run at around 40% of normal volume?
That's a reasonable way to frame it.
Got it. For the revenue, I’ll sum up the revenues made from holidays and working days.
Assuming that the holidays have about 0.4 times the traffic of working days. So the
revenue would be number of days times the total cars in day times the average toll.
Does that work?
Yes, that's a sensible way to manage complexity. Proceed.
Before I calculate, let me quickly restate the structure: first, I'll find vehicles per hour
by computing per-lane throughput and multiplying by all 6 lanes. Second, I'll convert
the three time blocks into effective peak-equivalent hours and multiply by hourly
throughput to get total daily vehicles. Third, I'll split that by the 4:1 LMV:HMV ratio and
apply the respective tolls to get daily revenue. Finally, I'll annualize across 365 days,
and sanity-check it against the weekday/holiday distinction we just discussed. Sounds
good?
Yes, go ahead.
Starting with lane throughput: at 20 seconds per vehicle, that's 3,600/20 = 180 vehicles
per lane per hour. Across all 6 lanes, that's 180 × 6 = 1,080 vehicles per hour at peak flow.
Converting our time blocks to effective hours:
8 + (5 × ½) + (11 × ⅙ ) ≈ 12.33 effective hours.
Total vehicles per day:
1,080 × 12.33 ≈ 13,320.
Splitting by the 4:1 ratio:
LMVs ≈ 10,656
HMVs ≈ 2,664.
Daily revenue:
(10,656 × ₹100) + (2,664 × ₹300)
= ₹18,64,800.
Therefore:
Annual Revenue
= ₹18,64,800 × 285 + ₹18,64,800*80*0.4
≈ ₹59 Cr.
Can you do a sanity check to verify your calculations?
Bandra-Worli Sea Link - Interview Transcript
Guesstimate | Transport | McKinsey & Co.
41
Okay. A clarifying question, what is Mumbai’s metro population and registered
vehicle count?
The population is around 20 million and vehicles count around 4 million.
Great.If even a small fraction, say 0.3-0.5% of the city's vehicle population crosses
the Sea Link on a given day, that works out to roughly 10,000-17,000 vehicles/day,
which lines up well with our estimate of ~13,320 vehicles/day. Given the Sea Link
primarily serves commuters between two specific high-traffic zones rather than
the whole city, a sub-1% daily crossing rate of the total vehicle base feels
directionally reasonable.
That's a thorough estimate with a solid range. Good work.
Yes, that's fair. Saturdays would still see decent business activity, but Sundays and
holidays would see a real dip.

title: Market Entry Strategy – Consumer Goods (FMCG)
question:
• How would you structure a market entry strategy for this client?
• What analysis would you prioritize, and why?
• What would your go-to-market plan look like across the three markets?
• How should the company sequence its entry into Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Market Entry 
Strategy
1. Market Entry Strategy – Consumer Goods (FMCG): How an Indian FMCG major can 
structure its expansion into Southeast Asia.
Introduction
An Indian FMCG major with a strong domestic presence is looking to expand into Southeast Asian markets, 
specifically Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Despite its scale and brand strength in India, the company has 
no prior international operating experience. This case study explores how such a company should structure a market 
entry strategy, including the analysis to prioritize and the go-to-market plan to follow.
Background
The Indian FMCG major has built its business on deep distribution networks, strong brand recall, and cost-efficient 
manufacturing within India. With domestic growth beginning to plateau in certain categories, the company's 
leadership has identified Southeast Asia as a natural next step, given the region's growing middle class, rising 
disposable incomes, and cultural and consumption similarities to India.
However, the company faces a limited understanding of local consumer behavior, differing regulatory regimes 
across Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines, and a competitive landscape already dominated by established local 
players and global FMCG giants. Without a structured entry strategy, the company risks costly missteps and slow 
market traction.
Structuring the Market Entry Strategy
• Market Attractiveness Screening- Rank Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines on market size, category 
growth rates, income distribution, and ease of doing business, to decide sequencing rather than entering all 
three simultaneously.
• Consumer Behavior Research- Conduct in-market research on purchasing habits, price sensitivity, preferred 
pack sizes, and channel preferences (general trade versus modern trade versus e-commerce) in each target 
country.
• Regulatory and Compliance Mapping- Assess import duties, local manufacturing incentives, labelling and 
product-registration requirements, and foreign ownership restrictions to determine the most viable legal 
structure.
• Competitive Landscape Assessment- Map incumbent local players and global competitors by category, 
pricing tier, and distribution reach to identify white spaces the company can credibly target.
• Entry Mode Evaluation- Weigh options such as export-led entry, joint ventures with local distributors, 
licensing, or greenfield investment, based on speed to market, capital intensity, and risk appetite.
• Phased Go-to-Market Plan- Start with a focused portfolio of two to three hero products in one lead market, 
build distribution and brand trust, then scale category breadth and geographic footprint in subsequent phases.
Impact
• Reduced Entry Risk- A phased, research-backed approach limits capital exposure while the company builds 
on-ground understanding before scaling.
• Faster Localization- Early investment in consumer and regulatory research helps the company adapt 
packaging, pricing, and messaging to local preferences more quickly than competitors entering blind.
• Sustainable Revenue Growth- A disciplined market and channel prioritization approach improves the odds 
of profitable, repeatable growth rather than one-off wins.
• Reusable Expansion Playbook- The frameworks and learnings from this first expansion create a template the 
company can reapply to future international markets.
Final Note
Successful market entry into Southeast Asia will depend on the company's ability to combine its domestic strengths 
in distribution and brand-building with rigorous, market-specific research. A staged approach that prioritizes 
learning before scale gives the company the best chance of establishing a durable presence in a competitive and 
unfamiliar landscape.
Questions for Discussion
• How would you structure a market entry strategy for this client?
• What analysis would you prioritize, and why?
• What would your go-to-market plan look like across the three markets?
• How should the company sequence its entry into Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines?

title: Cost Optimization – Telecom
question:
• How would you identify and prioritize cost-reduction opportunities across this business?
• Walk through your approach step by step.
• How would you ensure cost cuts do not compromise service quality?
• Which cost levers would you expect to deliver the fastest impact, and which would take longer?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Cost Optimization
2. Cost Optimization – Telecom: How a telecom operator can address margin pressure from 
declining ARPU and rising network costs.
Introduction
A telecom operator is facing significant margin pressure driven by declining average revenue per user (ARPU) and 
rising network operating expenses. This case study explores how the operator can identify and prioritize cost-
reduction opportunities across the business without compromising service quality.
Background
The operator's revenue per user has been steadily declining amid intense price competition and market saturation, 
while network operating expenses continue to climb due to rising data consumption, tower and energy costs, and 
expanding infrastructure requirements. Vendor contracts for network equipment, maintenance, and managed 
services were negotiated several years ago and have not been revisited.
There is currently no structured framework within the organization to systematically identify, evaluate, and 
prioritize cost-saving opportunities, and any past cost-cutting efforts have been ad hoc, raising concern that further 
cuts could degrade network quality and accelerate customer churn.
Approach to Identifying Cost-Reduction Opportunities
• Cost Baseline and Benchmarking- Build a detailed breakdown of network opex (energy, tower leases, 
maintenance, backhaul, managed services) and benchmark each line item against industry peers to size the 
opportunity.
• Vendor Contract Review- Audit existing vendor and managed-services contracts for outdated pricing, 
renegotiate volume-based discounts, and consider multi-vendor bidding to restore competitive tension.
• Network Infrastructure Optimization- Evaluate opportunities such as tower and site sharing with other 
operators, energy-efficient equipment upgrades, and decommissioning of redundant or underutilized sites.
• Zero-Based Cost Framework- Apply a zero-based budgeting lens to non-network costs (customer service, 
back-office, real estate) to challenge legacy spend rather than trimming incrementally.
• Impact vs. Effort Prioritization- Plot identified initiatives on an impact-versus-effort matrix, sequencing 
quick wins (vendor renegotiation) ahead of longer-term structural changes (infrastructure sharing).
• Quality Safeguards- Define minimum service-quality thresholds (network uptime, call drop rates, data 
speeds) that must be protected throughout implementation, with monitoring built into each initiative.
Impact
• Improved Margins- Renegotiated vendor contracts and infrastructure efficiencies directly reduce the cost 
base and help offset ARPU decline.
• Structured Decision-Making- A repeatable cost framework replaces ad hoc cuts, giving leadership a 
consistent way to evaluate future cost initiatives.
• Protected Service Quality- Built-in quality safeguards ensure cost reduction does not come at the expense of 
customer experience or churn.
• Stronger Vendor Leverage- A systematic contract review process improves the operator's negotiating 
position on an ongoing basis, not just as a one-time exercise.
Final Note
Addressing margin pressure in telecom requires more than isolated cost cuts. By combining vendor renegotiation, 
infrastructure optimization, and a disciplined prioritization framework, the operator can protect service quality while 
building a sustainable, repeatable approach to cost management.
Questions for Discussion
• How would you identify and prioritize cost-reduction opportunities across this business?
• Walk through your approach step by step.
• How would you ensure cost cuts do not compromise service quality?
• Which cost levers would you expect to deliver the fastest impact, and which would take longer?

title: Digital Transformation Roadmap – Banking
question:
• How would you design a digital transformation roadmap for this bank?
• What would you prioritize in year one versus year three?
• How should the bank balance quick wins against longer-term platform investments?
• What role should data and personalization play in the bank's strategy to retain younger customers?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Digital 
Transformation Roadmap
3. Digital Transformation Roadmap – Banking: How a mid-sized bank can compete with digital-
first fintechs and neo-banks.
Introduction
A mid-sized bank is losing younger customers to digital-first fintech competitors and neo-banks that offer seamless 
mobile experiences. This case study explores how the bank can design a digital transformation roadmap, prioritizing 
the right initiatives across a multi-year horizon.
Background
The bank has a loyal base of older customers built on branch relationships and traditional trust, but its digital 
initiatives have been fragmented across departments, with no unified strategy guiding investment. The mobile app is 
outdated relative to fintech competitors, offering limited functionality and a clunky user experience.
The bank also makes limited use of the customer data it already holds, missing opportunities for personalization that 
neo-banks use effectively to deepen engagement. As younger, digitally native customers increasingly choose fintech 
alternatives for everyday banking, the bank risks losing an entire generation of future customers.
Designing the Digital Transformation Roadmap
• Digital Maturity Assessment- Audit existing digital initiatives, technology stack, and customer journeys to 
identify gaps against leading fintech and neo-bank experiences.
• Unified Digital Strategy- Consolidate fragmented initiatives under a single roadmap with clear ownership, 
replacing siloed departmental efforts with a coordinated, bank-wide program.
• Core Mobile Experience Overhaul- Prioritize a rebuilt mobile app with essential, high-frequency features 
(instant transfers, spend tracking, simple onboarding) delivered early to stop customer attrition.
• Data-Driven Personalization- Invest in a customer data platform that unifies transaction and behavioral data 
to enable targeted offers, personalized product recommendations, and proactive service.
• Talent and Partnerships- Build internal digital product and engineering capability while selectively 
partnering with fintechs for capabilities that would take too long to build in-house.
• Phased Roadmap- Sequence initiatives across a three-year horizon, balancing quick, visible wins in year one 
with deeper platform and data investments by year three.
Impact
• Slowed Customer Attrition- A modernized mobile experience addresses the most visible gap driving 
younger customers to competitors.
• Improved Engagement- Data-driven personalization increases relevance of offers and products, deepening 
customer relationships over time.
• Coordinated Execution- A unified roadmap eliminates duplicated effort and ensures digital investment is 
directed toward the highest-impact initiatives.
• Long-Term Competitiveness- Building internal digital capability, supported by targeted partnerships, 
positions the bank to keep pace with fintech innovation beyond the initial roadmap.
Final Note
Competing with digital-first fintechs requires the bank to move beyond fragmented digital projects toward a 
coordinated, customer-centric transformation. By prioritizing a strong core mobile experience early and building 
toward deeper data and platform capabilities over three years, the bank can defend its customer base while laying the 
foundation for long-term digital competitiveness.
Questions for Discussion
• How would you design a digital transformation roadmap for this bank?
• What would you prioritize in year one versus year three?
• How should the bank balance quick wins against longer-term platform investments?
• What role should data and personalization play in the bank's strategy to retain younger customers?

title: Organizational Restructuring – Manufacturing
question:
• How can companies balance the need for aggressive cost synergies with the risk 
of damaging employee morale during a restructuring? 
• What specific metrics should leadership use to objectively evaluate candidates 
when deciding between two employees for a single consolidated role? 
• How does an undefined or poorly communicated operating model contribute to 
post-merger integration failure? 
• What role does transparent communication play in mitigating productivity loss 
during the uncertainty of an organizational redesign?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Organizational Restructuring – Manufacturing 
4. How a manufacturing company redesigned its organizational structure post-merger 
to resolve role overlaps and realize cost synergies. 
Introduction A prominent manufacturing company recently completed a major 
acquisition aimed at driving growth and market consolidation. However, the integration 
process resulted in overlapping departments, duplicated roles, and unclear reporting 
lines. This case study explores the organizational redesign strategy implemented to 
resolve these post-merger challenges, streamline operations, and capture intended 
financial benefits. 
Background Following the acquisition, the combined entity struggled with severe 
structural inefficiencies. The presence of redundant roles across the legacy and 
acquired companies led to intense role ambiguity. Consequently, the organization 
experienced slow decision-making, plummeting employee morale, and failed to realize 
the projected cost synergies from the merger, necessitating an immediate restructuring 
intervention. 
Restructuring Strategies 
• Operating Model Alignment: The company first defined the future-state 
operating model to ensure the new structure supported the combined entity's 
strategic goals. This involved centralizing shared services (like HR, Finance, and 
IT) to reduce redundancies, while decentralizing plant operations to maintain 
local agility. 
• Role Mapping and 'Spans and Layers' Framework: The organization applied a 
"Spans and Layers" framework to audit reporting lines. By mapping out 
overlapping roles, they aimed to widen the span of control (the number of direct 
reports per manager) and reduce unnecessary hierarchical layers to accelerate 
decision-making. 
• Competency and Skills Assessment (The "Best Fit" Approach): To resolve role 
overlaps objectively, the company utilized competency matrices and 
performance metrics. Employees in duplicated roles were evaluated based on 
future-state requirements, ensuring the most qualified individuals were retained 
or reassigned regardless of their legacy company affiliation. 
• Change Management and Transparent Communication: A robust 
communication plan was established to address employee anxieties. This 
included clear timelines for the restructuring, transparent criteria for role 
selection, and transition support/severance packages for displaced workers to 
protect the morale of the remaining staff. 
Impact 
• Accelerated Decision-Making: Streamlined reporting lines and reduced 
hierarchical layers eliminated bottlenecks, allowing for faster, more agile 
operational and strategic decisions. 
• Realized Cost Synergies: Consolidating overlapping departments and 
eliminating duplicated roles significantly reduced overhead costs, enabling the 
company to achieve the merger's financial targets. 
• Improved Employee Morale: Clear role definitions, transparent 
communication, and structured reporting lines removed ambiguity, restoring 
employee confidence and daily productivity. 
• Operational Efficiency: A unified operating model ensured that both legacy and 
acquired manufacturing units worked cohesively under a single, standardized 
framework. 
Final Note This restructuring initiative demonstrates that a successful merger extends 
beyond financial transactions into complex human capital and structural integration. By 
applying objective frameworks to resolve role overlaps and aligning the organization 
with a clear operating model, the manufacturing company successfully navigated post-
merger turbulence to unlock its true synergistic value. 
Questions for Discussion 
• How can companies balance the need for aggressive cost synergies with the risk 
of damaging employee morale during a restructuring? 
• What specific metrics should leadership use to objectively evaluate candidates 
when deciding between two employees for a single consolidated role? 
• How does an undefined or poorly communicated operating model contribute to 
post-merger integration failure? 
• What role does transparent communication play in mitigating productivity loss 
during the uncertainty of an organizational redesign?

title: Supply Chain Optimization – Retail
question:
• How does the shift from a centralized distribution model to a multi-echelon 
network impact overall transportation and warehousing costs? 
• What are the key data points required to build a highly accurate, predictive 
demand forecasting model for retail? 
• How can a retailer handle sudden shifts in consumer demand that historical 
data might fail to predict (e.g., unexpected viral trends)? 
• What are the operational risks of relying too heavily on automated replenishment 
systems without human oversight?
solution_approach:
Case Study on Supply Chain Optimization – Retail 
5. How a large retail chain redesigned its supply chain to balance inventory, reduce 
stockouts, and improve demand forecasting. 
Introduction A large retail chain operating over 200 stores faced significant logistical 
challenges, struggling to maintain appropriate stock levels across its network. The 
company experienced frequent stockouts of fast-moving consumer goods alongside an 
accumulation of slow-moving excess inventory. This case study analyzes the supply 
chain optimization strategies used to redesign their distribution model and balance 
inventory. 
Background Before the optimization effort, the retailer relied heavily on a rigid, 
centralized distribution model and rudimentary demand forecasting methods. This 
setup caused long lead times for store replenishment. The inability to accurately predict 
local store demand resulted in a severe mismatch of inventory levels, frustrating 
customers with empty shelves for popular items while tying up capital in stagnant 
regional warehouse stock. 
Optimization Strategies 
• Predictive Demand Forecasting: The retailer leveraged historical sales data, 
local seasonal trends, and external variables (such as local events or weather) 
using machine learning algorithms. This shifted forecasting from a regional 
aggregate to highly accurate, localized predictions at the individual store level. 
• Hub-and-Spoke Distribution Redesign: The company transitioned from a 
strictly centralized model to a multi-echelon "hub-and-spoke" network. They 
introduced smaller, localized fulfillment centers closer to high-density store 
clusters to drastically reduce replenishment lead times. 
• Automated Replenishment and Min/Max Levers: Dynamic Min/Max inventory 
levers driven by real-time Point of Sale (POS) data were implemented. This 
system triggered automatic reordering for fast-moving items just in time, 
preventing stockouts without over-ordering. 
• SKU Rationalization and Redistribution: By analyzing inventory turnover ratios, 
the supply chain team identified slow-moving products (SKUs). They initiated 
targeted markdowns and dynamically redistributed excess stock from regional 
warehouses to specific stores where localized demand for those specific items 
was higher. 
 
 
Impact 
• Reduced Stockouts: Real-time data integration and localized forecasting 
drastically decreased the out-of-stock rate for high-velocity items, directly 
increasing top-line revenue and customer trust. 
• Optimized Inventory Capital: Redistributing and rationalizing slow-moving 
items freed up valuable working capital and reduced warehousing holding costs. 
• Shortened Lead Times: The decentralized, multi-echelon distribution network 
allowed for agile, and in some cases same-day, replenishment for critical stock. 
• Enhanced Customer Satisfaction: Consistent product availability improved the 
overall shopping experience, driving repeat foot traffic and brand loyalty. 
Final Note The retailer's turnaround highlights the critical shift from a push-based, 
centralized supply chain to a pull-based, data-driven network. By leveraging advanced 
analytics for forecasting and decentralizing distribution, the company successfully 
aligned its inventory levels with actual consumer demand, transforming a logistical 
liability into a competitive advantage. 
Questions for Discussion 
• How does the shift from a centralized distribution model to a multi-echelon 
network impact overall transportation and warehousing costs? 
• What are the key data points required to build a highly accurate, predictive 
demand forecasting model for retail? 
• How can a retailer handle sudden shifts in consumer demand that historical 
data might fail to predict (e.g., unexpected viral trends)? 
• What are the operational risks of relying too heavily on automated replenishment 
systems without human oversight?

title: M&A Due Diligence – Telecom
question:
• Why might a target company in the telecom sector intentionally defer 
infrastructure maintenance prior to seeking an acquisition? 
• How does discovering significant "technical debt" during due diligence directly 
impact the final valuation and negotiation strategy of a deal? 
• What steps can an acquiring company take to protect itself if it discovers minor 
regulatory non-compliance during the final stages of due diligence? 
• How should the acquiring company balance the urgency to close a competitive 
deal with the thoroughness required for a comprehensive due diligence process?
solution_approach:
Case Study on M&A Due Diligence – Telecom 
6. How a national telecom company conducted comprehensive due diligence to 
evaluate the acquisition of a regional ISP and mitigate hidden risks. 
Introduction A leading national telecom company sought to rapidly expand its 
broadband footprint and customer base by evaluating the acquisition of a regional 
Internet Service Provider (ISP). While the target company presented highly attractive 
financial metrics on the surface, the acquirer needed to validate the deal's true value. 
This case study details the due diligence approach utilized to uncover hidden liabilities, 
assess regulatory compliance, and validate infrastructure quality. 
Background The telecommunications sector is highly capital-intensive and heavily 
regulated. Prior to initiating formal due diligence, the national telecom company noted 
that the regional ISP's reported profit margins were unusually high compared to industry 
benchmarks. This raised initial concerns regarding potential underinvestment in 
network maintenance, hidden operational liabilities, and regulatory compliance gaps 
that could jeopardize the acquisition's long-term viability. 
Due Diligence Approach & Red Flags 
• Technical and Infrastructure Assessment: The company deployed network 
engineers to audit the quality, age, and capacity of the physical broadband 
infrastructure (e.g., fiber versus legacy copper wiring). Red flags targeted: 
Deferred maintenance, outdated hardware nearing end-of-life, or a lack of 
scalability to support future bandwidth demands. 
• Quality of Earnings (QoE) Analysis: Financial experts conducted a deep dive to 
normalize EBITDA and verify the sustainability of revenue streams. Red flags 
targeted: Premature revenue recognition, high customer churn rates masked by 
aggressive short-term promotional discounting, or massive off-balance-sheet 
liabilities. 
• Regulatory and Legal Compliance Audit: Legal teams reviewed local municipal 
agreements, right-of-way access rights, and spectrum licenses. Red flags 
targeted: Pending litigation, expiring local permits, or non-compliance with data 
privacy regulations. 
• Customer and Contract Diligence: The team reviewed the terms of enterprise 
contracts and analyzed the retail customer base for satisfaction and retention 
metrics. Red flags targeted: A high concentration of revenue tied to a few easily 
terminable enterprise contracts, or a history of frequent network outages leading 
to poor customer reviews. 
 
Impact 
• Risk Mitigation: The multi-pronged due diligence approach successfully 
identified areas where the regional ISP had deferred maintenance, allowing the

evaluate the acquisition of a regional ISP and mitigate hidden risks. 
Introduction A leading national telecom company sought to rapidly expand its 
broadband footprint and customer base by evaluating the acquisition of a regional 
Internet Service Provider (ISP). While the target company presented highly attractive 
financial metrics on the surface, the acquirer needed to validate the deal's true value. 
This case study details the due diligence approach utilized to uncover hidden liabilities, 
assess regulatory compliance, and validate infrastructure quality. 
Background The telecommunications sector is highly capital-intensive and heavily 
regulated. Prior to initiating formal due diligence, the national telecom company noted 
that the regional ISP's reported profit margins were unusually high compared to industry 
benchmarks. This raised initial concerns regarding potential underinvestment in 
network maintenance, hidden operational liabilities, and regulatory compliance gaps 
that could jeopardize the acquisition's long-term viability. 
Due Diligence Approach & Red Flags 
• Technical and Infrastructure Assessment: The company deployed network 
engineers to audit the quality, age, and capacity of the physical broadband 
infrastructure (e.g., fiber versus legacy copper wiring). Red flags targeted: 
Deferred maintenance, outdated hardware nearing end-of-life, or a lack of 
scalability to support future bandwidth demands. 
• Quality of Earnings (QoE) Analysis: Financial experts conducted a deep dive to 
normalize EBITDA and verify the sustainability of revenue streams. Red flags 
targeted: Premature revenue recognition, high customer churn rates masked by 
aggressive short-term promotional discounting, or massive off-balance-sheet 
liabilities. 
• Regulatory and Legal Compliance Audit: Legal teams reviewed local municipal 
agreements, right-of-way access rights, and spectrum licenses. Red flags 
targeted: Pending litigation, expiring local permits, or non-compliance with data 
privacy regulations. 
• Customer and Contract Diligence: The team reviewed the terms of enterprise 
contracts and analyzed the retail customer base for satisfaction and retention 
metrics. Red flags targeted: A high concentration of revenue tied to a few easily 
terminable enterprise contracts, or a history of frequent network outages leading 
to poor customer reviews.

identified areas where the regional ISP had deferred maintenance, allowing the 
acquirer to forecast and prepare for necessary capital expenditures post-merger.

cost of upgrading legacy hardware (technical debt), the national telecom 
company was able to negotiate a fairer, reduced purchase price.

agreements ensured that expansion plans would not be halted by legal 
injunctions post-acquisition.

budget for integrating the regional infrastructure into its national network.

validating high-stakes M&A transactions, particularly in asset-heavy industries like 
telecommunications. A rigorous, cross-functional due diligence approach—spanning 
financial, technical, and legal domains—is essential to uncover red flags, accurately

Phase 3 — Target Operating Model & Roadmap Design 
With priorities set, the team designs the target operating model — governance bodies, decision rights, funding

Phase 4 — Technology & Data Architecture Design 
This phase defines the reference architecture: a unified cloud data platform, master data management standards, 
and interoperability protocols (including healthcare data standards such as HL7 FHIR) that allow the prioritized 
use cases to be built on common foundations rather than one-off integrations. 
Phase 5 — Pilot Execution and Scaling 
Selected initiatives are piloted in controlled scope, validated against predefined success metrics, and then 
scaled deliberately — avoiding both premature scaling of unproven concepts and indefinite pilot purgatory. 
Phase 6 — Governance, Talent, and Continuous Improvement

development — that allows the digital portfolio to evolve as market conditions, regulation, and technology 
continue to change. 
3. Key Considerations for the Board 
The Board will likely ask how the strategy avoids becoming another wave of disconnected pilots. The answer 
lies in the prioritization discipline of Phase 2 and the operating model established in Phase 3: initiatives are 
funded and governed as a portfolio, not approved individually based on whichever function advocates most 
persuasively. 
A second likely concern is pace: pharmaceutical organizations operate under regulatory constraints that can 
slow technology adoption relative to other industries. The roadmap is deliberately structured with regulatory 
and compliance review built into each stage gate, rather than treated as a final hurdle after solutions are built. 
The Board will also want clarity on return on investment. Upfront investment in shared data infrastructure is 
significant, but the long-term benefit is that each subsequent use case is built faster and at lower marginal cost 
— the economics improve as the portfolio matures. 
Expected business outcomes: 
• Faster, more consistent commercial engagement across HCP and patient channels 
• Reduced cycle time from data collection to R&D and real-world-evidence insight 
• Improved manufacturing responsiveness to demand volatility 
Potential implementation challenges: 
• Resistance to change from functions accustomed to independent technology budgets 
• Data privacy and security requirements across multiple jurisdictions 
• Legacy system dependencies that complicate near-term integration 
Relevant Critical Success Factors and KPIs: 
• Time-to-insight for R&D and real-world evidence generation 
• Commercial cost-to-serve per HCP / patient interaction 
• Percentage of digital initiatives meeting stage-gate value targets 
• Data platform adoption rate across business functions 
4. Sample Deliverables 
• Digital Opportunity Prioritization Matrix (Excel) 
• Digital Transformation Roadmap (PowerPoint) 
• Target Operating Model Blueprint (PowerPoint / Word) 
• Business Case & Value Tracking Model (Excel) 
• Data Governance & Interoperability Playbook (PDF) 
• Digital KPI Dashboard Template (Excel) 
5. Strategic Alignment with Corporate Strategy 
Digital transformation is not pursued as a standalone initiative; it must be explicitly linked to the corporate 
growth strategy — whether that strategy emphasizes specialty pipeline expansion, geographic growth, or 
margin improvement ahead of anticipated biosimilar competition. Each element of the digital roadmap is 
mapped back to the corporate strategic priority it advances, which keeps prioritization decisions grounded in 
enterprise value rather than functional preference. 
6. Culture and Change Leadership 
Digital transformation in a historically siloed organization succeeds or fails on leadership behavior. Executives 
across R&D, commercial, and manufacturing must visibly sponsor cross-functional initiatives and be willing to 
reallocate budget and talent away from legacy, function-specific systems. Incentive structures are adjusted so 
that functional leaders are rewarded for enterprise outcomes — such as faster time-to-insight — rather than for 
the size of their independent technology budget. 
7. Technology and Data Architecture Enablement 
A unified cloud data platform and common data model are the foundation on which prioritized use cases are 
built — from AI-assisted real-world evidence generation in R&D, to next-best-action engagement models in 
commercial, to predictive demand sensing in manufacturing. Interoperability standards, including healthcare-
specific protocols such as HL7 FHIR, ensure that data generated in one function can be trusted and reused by 
another, rather than re-collected and reconciled department by department. 
8. Regulatory and Compliance Landscape 
Data privacy and clinical data-handling requirements (including HIPAA, GDPR, and evolving FDA guidance 
on AI-enabled tools) shape both the pace and the architecture of the transformation. Rather than treating 
compliance as a constraint to be managed at the end of each project, the strategy embeds regulatory and 
privacy review at each stage gate — turning disciplined compliance into a source of competitive advantage and 
trust with regulators, physicians, and patients, rather than a source of delay. 
9. Opportunity Identification and Prioritization 
Opportunity identification combines structured workshops across R&D, medical affairs, commercial, and 
manufacturing with a quantitative scoring model that weighs strategic value, feasibility, and time-to-value. This 
produces a two-by-two prioritization view that distinguishes quick wins from foundational, longer-horizon 
investments — for example, a next-best-action commercial engagement tool might score high on both value 
and near-term feasibility, while an enterprise real-world-evidence platform scores high on value but requires 
the shared data architecture to be in place first. 
10. Cost-Benefit Analysis and Business Case Development 
Each initiative in the portfolio carries its own business case, weighing upfront technology and change-
management investment against quantifiable benefits — commercial revenue uplift, R&D cycle-time 
reduction, and manufacturing cost avoidance — as well as harder-to-quantify benefits such as regulatory 
goodwill and improved physician trust. Shared infrastructure investments, such as the common data platform, 
are evaluated as enablers whose return is realized across multiple downstream use cases rather than judged 
against a single initiative in isolation. 
11. Monitoring, Governance, and KPIs 
A digital steering committee, chaired jointly by the Chief Strategy Officer and Chief Digital Officer, reviews 
the initiative portfolio against stage-gate criteria on a quarterly cadence. A KPI dashboard tracks leading 
indicators — data platform adoption, initiative cycle time — alongside lagging indicators such as commercial 
cost-to-serve, giving the organization an early warning system rather than a year-end scorecard. 
12. Cross-Functional Integration 
The clearest illustration of cross-functional integration is a new specialty product launch, which requires 
clinical trial data, medical affairs insight, market access evidence, and manufacturing forecasts to be 
synchronized rather than assembled independently by each function. A digital "control tower" view, built on 
the common data platform, gives launch teams shared visibility into these interdependent workstreams — 
surfacing risks, such as a manufacturing capacity constraint, before they affect the launch timeline. 
13. Return on Investment 
The return on investment for enterprise digital transformation in specialty pharmaceuticals is realized on two 
timelines. In the near term, targeted use cases such as commercial engagement optimization generate 
measurable value within two to three quarters. In the medium term, the shared data and operating model 
foundation reduces the marginal cost of each subsequent initiative, compounding returns as the portfolio 
matures. Industry analyses of digital maturity in pharmaceutical commercial and R&D operations suggest that 
top-quartile digital adopters achieve meaningfully lower cost-to-serve and faster time to insight than peers who 
pursue digital investment on a system-by-system basis — consistent with the outcomes targeted in this 
engagement. 
14. Building a Digitally-Fluent Culture 
Sustaining transformation requires building digital fluency well beyond the technology function. Structured 
training equips commercial, medical, and manufacturing teams to interpret and act on the insights the new 
platforms generate, rather than treating dashboards as something only data teams understand. Rotational 
assignments that embed business talent within digital delivery teams, and vice versa, help dissolve the 
historical divide between "the business" and "IT" that the diagnostic phase identified as a root cause of 
fragmentation. 
15. Key Findings and Recommendations 
• Treat digital transformation as a prioritized portfolio governed against enterprise value — not a collection 
of independently sponsored pilots. 
• Invest in shared data architecture and interoperability standards early; they are the foundation that lowers 
the marginal cost of every subsequent initiative. 
• Redesign the operating model — governance, funding, and incentives — alongside the technology, since 
operating-model gaps, not technology gaps, are the more common cause of stalled digital initiatives. 
• Embed regulatory and data-privacy review into each stage gate rather than at the end of delivery, turning 
compliance into a source of trust rather than delay. 
• Sequence initiatives to pair near-term, high-feasibility wins with the longer-horizon foundational 
investments they ultimately depend on, sustaining executive and Board confidence through the multi-year 
roadmap.

workflows, reducing no-show rates from 22% to 11%, cutting average scheduling call time from 8 
minutes to under 2, and increasing telehealth utilization from 9% to 34% of eligible visits within 12 
months.

● Change Management Playbook 
● Additional Considerations 
● Key Findings and FAQs 
1. Background 
A regional healthcare network operating 18 primary and specialty care clinics had invested in telehealth 
capability during a prior initiative, but utilization remained low at just 9% of eligible visits — well below 
the network's own targets and below regional peer benchmarks. Meanwhile, appointment no-show 
rates sat at 22%, driven partly by a phone-only scheduling process with average call wait times of eight 
minutes, which discouraged patients from calling back to reschedule or confirm appointments. 
Clinic staff reported that patients frequently didn't know telehealth was an available option for their 
visit type, and that the scheduling phone line was overwhelmed during peak hours, pushing some 
patients to simply not show up rather than wait on hold. Leadership needed to determine whether 
investment should focus on promoting the existing telehealth capability more heavily, or on a broader 
redesign of the patient scheduling and communication experience that telehealth adoption depended 
on. 
2. Methodology 
A 6-phase digital transformation approach was applied: 
● Phase 1 – Patient Journey Diagnostic: Map the scheduling, reminder, and visit journey to 
identify where patients disengaged or defaulted to no-show. 
● Phase 2 – Telehealth Eligibility Analysis: Determine which visit types were clinically appropriate 
for telehealth and why eligible patients weren't choosing it. 
● Phase 3 – Digital Scheduling Redesign: Build an online scheduling option integrated with clinic 
calendars, reducing dependence on phone-based booking. 
● Phase 4 – Communication Redesign: Implement automated, multi-channel appointment 
reminders and telehealth-option prompts at the point of scheduling. 
● Phase 5 – Phased Clinic Rollout: Pilot the redesigned experience at a subset of clinics before 
network-wide deployment. 
● Phase 6 – Scale & Optimize: Expand to all clinics and continuously refine based on no-show and 
utilization data. 
3. Key Considerations 
● Low telehealth utilization wasn't primarily an awareness problem — it was a default problem: 
patients weren't being offered telehealth as an option at the point of scheduling for eligible visit 
types. 
● No-show rates were closely tied to scheduling friction; patients who couldn't easily reschedule 
when their circumstances changed simply didn't show up rather than navigating a long phone 
wait. 
● Older patient populations required a digital scheduling experience that didn't assume high 
digital literacy, alongside continued phone support rather than a phone-line replacement.

● Patient journey diagnostic with no-show driver analysis 
● Telehealth eligibility criteria and default-offer framework 
● Online scheduling platform integration plan 
● Automated multi-channel reminder and communication workflow 
● Clinic-level rollout and adoption tracking dashboard 
5. Strategic Recommendations 
The recommended approach centered on three changes: (1) implementing online self-scheduling 
integrated with clinic calendars to reduce dependence on the overwhelmed phone line; (2) defaulting 
eligible visit types to offer telehealth as an explicit choice at the point of scheduling rather than 
requiring patients to ask for it; and (3) replacing single-channel appointment reminders with automated 
text, email, and app notifications including one-tap rescheduling. 
6. Culture and Change Management 
Clinic front-desk staff were concerned that online scheduling would reduce their role and create 
confusion if patients booked inappropriate appointment types. The program addressed this by 
positioning online scheduling as a capacity release valve for phone staff — reducing call volume so staff 
could spend more time on complex scheduling needs and patient support — with clear escalation paths 
built into the online system for ambiguous cases. 
7. Technology and Platform Architecture 
An online scheduling platform was integrated directly with existing clinic calendar systems, allowing 
real-time appointment booking without manual reconciliation by front-desk staff. Automated 
communication workflows were layered on top to handle reminders and telehealth prompts based on 
visit type and patient history. 
8. Patient Journey Redesign 
The scheduling journey was redesigned so that telehealth-eligible visit types presented telehealth as a 
default, equally prominent option alongside in-person scheduling, rather than an obscure alternative 
patients had to specifically request. 
9. Regulatory and Privacy Considerations 
The telehealth and digital scheduling platforms were implemented in full compliance with applicable 
healthcare privacy regulations, with particular attention to secure video-visit infrastructure and patient 
data handling across the newly integrated scheduling and communication systems. 
10. Risk Identification 
Key risks included the possibility of increased no-shows if online scheduling made booking too 
frictionless without adequate reminder follow-up, clinical risk if patients selected telehealth for visit 
types requiring in-person examination, and the risk of alienating less digitally comfortable patients. Each 
was mitigated through automated reminder sequencing, clinically validated eligibility rules, and 
continued phone-support availability. 
11. Cost-Benefit Analysis 
Platform investment was weighed against the value of reduced no-show-related revenue loss, reduced 
phone-staffing pressure, and better utilization of existing telehealth infrastructure that had already been 
paid for but underused. The business case showed payback within the first year primarily through no-
show reduction. 
12. Monitoring and Adoption Metrics 
No-show rate, average scheduling call time, telehealth utilization rate, and online scheduling adoption 
were tracked weekly during the pilot phase, allowing rapid identification of clinics or visit types where 
the redesigned journey wasn't performing as expected. 
13. Integration with Clinical Systems 
The scheduling and communication platforms were integrated with the network's electronic health 
record (EHR) system to ensure visit-type eligibility rules and patient history were reflected accurately in 
real time, avoiding scheduling errors that could create clinical risk. 
14. Return on Investment 
Within 12 months, no-show rates fell from 22% to 11%, average scheduling call time dropped from eight 
minutes to under two, and telehealth utilization rose from 9% to 34% of eligible visits, substantially 
improving both patient access and clinic operational efficiency. 
15. Establishing a Digital Operating Model 
A Patient Digital Experience team was established, combining clinical operations, IT, and patient 
communications representation, to sustain ongoing optimization of scheduling and telehealth adoption 
beyond the initial rollout. 
16. Change Management Playbook 
A playbook was developed for front-desk staff transitioning toward higher-value patient support roles, 
along with a phased clinic rollout sequence and patient communication materials introducing the new 
scheduling and telehealth options. 
17. Additional Considerations 
The platform architecture was designed to support future expansion into chronic condition remote 
monitoring and asynchronous digital visits, building on the scheduling and communication foundation 
established in this phase. 
18. Key Findings and FAQs 
Why was telehealth utilization so low despite prior investment? Because eligible visit types weren't 
defaulting patients toward the telehealth option at the point of scheduling — the capability existed but 
wasn't being actively offered. 
What had the single biggest impact on no-show reduction? Automated, multi-channel reminders with 
one-tap rescheduling, which let patients easily adjust plans instead of simply not showing up. 
How was clinical safety maintained while expanding telehealth defaults? Through clinically validated 
eligibility rules embedded directly into the scheduling system, ensuring only appropriate visit types were 
offered telehealth by default.

title: Customer Experience Overhaul for a Telecom Operator
question: Analyze the following business challenge: Customer Experience Overhaul for a Telecom Operator. Outline your structured approach, root cause diagnosis, and recommendations.
solution_approach:
Digital Network Modernization & 
Customer Experience Overhaul for a 
Telecom Operator 
Consulting Case Study | Telecom Industry 
Reading time: 9 minutes 
Executive Summary (TLDR) 
A national telecom operator was losing postpaid subscribers to a smaller, digitally native competitor 
despite having superior network coverage. Legacy OSS/BSS systems, slow provisioning times, and a 
fragmented customer experience across app, call center, and retail were driving churn. A structured 
network-and-CX transformation program cut new-service provisioning time from 5 days to 4 hours, 
reduced churn by 1.8 percentage points, and lifted digital self-service adoption from 31% to 58% within 
15 months. 
Table of Contents 
● Background 
● Methodology 
● Key Considerations 
● Sample Deliverables 
● Strategic Recommendations 
● Culture and Change Management 
● Technology and OSS/BSS Modernization 
● Operational Efficiency 
● Regulatory Considerations 
● Risk Identification 
● Cost-Benefit Analysis 
● Monitoring and KPIs 
● Integration Roadmap 
● Return on Investment 
● Establishing Governance 
● Implementation Playbook 
● Additional Considerations 
● Key Findings and FAQs 
1. Background 
A national telecom operator with strong network coverage and brand recognition began losing postpaid 
subscribers at an accelerating rate — down 1.8 points in market share over six quarters — despite 
consistently outperforming competitors in network quality surveys. Customer research revealed the 
issue wasn't the network; it was everything around it. Activating a new line took up to five business days 
due to manual provisioning steps across disconnected legacy OSS (Operations Support Systems) and BSS 
(Business Support Systems). Customers switching plans often experienced billing errors for one to two 
cycles. The mobile app covered only basic functions, pushing most service requests to call centers with 
average wait times exceeding 12 minutes. 
A smaller, digitally native competitor with weaker network coverage was winning switchers specifically 
because activation, plan changes, and support were instant and self-service. Leadership needed to 
determine whether to prioritize a full OSS/BSS replacement — expensive and high-risk — or a more 
targeted modernization of the systems and journeys causing the most customer pain. 
2. Methodology 
A 6-phase approach combining operational and digital transformation methodology was applied: 
● Phase 1 – Diagnostic & Journey Mapping: Quantify friction points across activation, plan 
changes, billing, and support using both system data and customer interviews. 
● Phase 2 – Prioritization: Rank pain points by combined customer impact and technical 
feasibility, rather than pursuing a full system replacement. 
● Phase 3 – Target Architecture Design: Design a modernized provisioning layer that could sit 
atop legacy OSS/BSS via APIs, avoiding a full "rip and replace." 
● Phase 4 – Journey Redesign: Rebuild the top five customer journeys (activation, plan change, 
billing dispute, device upgrade, outage reporting) for digital-first resolution. 
● Phase 5 – Phased Rollout: Deploy market-by-market to manage risk and capture learnings 
before national rollout. 
● Phase 6 – Scale & Optimize: Expand successful patterns nationally and retire redundant manual 
processes. 
3. Key Considerations 
● A full legacy system replacement was rejected as too risky and slow given competitive pressure; 
an API-layer approach delivered most of the customer-facing benefit at a fraction of the cost 
and time. 
● Provisioning delays were traced to seven manual handoff points between systems that had 
accumulated over a decade of incremental patches — the fix required both technology and 
process redesign. 
● Call-center staff needed a clear transition plan, since reduced call volume from improved self-
service directly affected their role. 
4. Sample Deliverables 
● Customer journey friction diagnostic and prioritization matrix 
● API-layer target architecture blueprint (legacy-compatible) 
● Redesigned digital journeys for activation, plan change, billing, and support 
● Phased market rollout plan with success criteria per wave 
● Call-center transition and reskilling plan 
5. Strategic Recommendations 
The recommended path avoided a full OSS/BSS replacement in favor of an API orchestration layer that 
automated the manual handoffs causing provisioning delays, paired with a redesigned mobile app 
covering the top customer journeys end-to-end. This combination addressed 80% of customer pain 
points within a fraction of the time and cost of full system replacement, while preserving the option for 
deeper modernization later. 
6. Culture and Change Management 
Call-center leadership initially resisted the shift toward self-service, viewing reduced call volume as a 
threat to their teams. The program reframed the transition around redeploying staff toward complex, 
high-value support cases — the ones self-service couldn't resolve — with a structured reskilling plan 
rather than headcount reduction, which secured buy-in from frontline leadership. 
7. Technology and OSS/BSS Modernization 
Rather than replacing legacy OSS/BSS systems outright, an orchestration layer was built to automate the 
seven manual handoff points in the provisioning process, cutting activation time from five days to under 
four hours while legacy systems remained the system of record underneath. 
8. Operational Efficiency 
Automating manual provisioning steps eliminated a significant volume of internal rework caused by 
human error in the handoff process, which had previously been a major driver of billing disputes in the 
first two cycles after any account change. 
9. Regulatory Considerations 
Billing accuracy improvements were tracked against regulatory requirements for consumer billing 
transparency, with the redesigned billing dispute journey built to meet documented resolution-timeline 
requirements consistently, which had previously been missed during peak volume periods. 
10. Risk Identification 
Key risks included the possibility of new customer-facing bugs during phased rollout, the risk of over-
automating and removing necessary human judgment in edge cases, and the risk of call-center attrition 
if the transition plan wasn't communicated clearly. Each was mitigated through phased deployment, 
defined escalation paths, and early, transparent staff communication. 
11. Cost-Benefit Analysis 
The API orchestration approach cost roughly a third of a full OSS/BSS replacement while delivering the 
majority of customer-facing improvement. The business case showed payback within 18 months driven 
by reduced churn and lower call-center cost-to-serve. 
12. Monitoring and KPIs 
Core KPIs tracked weekly included activation time, digital self-service adoption rate, first-cycle billing 
accuracy, call-center volume, and churn rate — allowing the team to validate impact market by market 
before national rollout. 
13. Integration Roadmap 
Rollout proceeded in three waves — two pilot markets, a mid-size regional expansion, and finally 
national deployment — with each wave's KPIs reviewed before proceeding, allowing course correction 
on journey design based on real usage data. 
14. Return on Investment 
Within 15 months, provisioning time dropped from five days to four hours, churn improved by 1.8 
percentage points, and digital self-service adoption rose from 31% to 58%, with call-center cost-to-serve 
down significantly as a result. 
15. Establishing Governance 
A joint IT-Operations-Customer Experience steering committee was established to own the 
transformation, ensuring technology, process, and frontline considerations were represented in every 
major rollout decision. 
16. Implementation Playbook 
A standardized market-rollout playbook was created covering technical deployment checklists, staff 
training sequencing, and customer communication timing, reducing variability in how each new market 
wave was executed. 
17. Additional Considerations 
The orchestration-layer approach was explicitly designed to be a stepping stone — architected so that a 
future full OSS/BSS modernization, if pursued, could build on the same API layer rather than requiring 
another disruptive redesign. 
18. Key Findings and FAQs 
Why not replace the legacy systems outright? The risk, cost, and timeline of a full replacement didn't 
match the urgency of the competitive threat; the orchestration-layer approach delivered comparable 
customer impact far faster. 
What was the single biggest driver of churn reduction? Faster activation and plan-change times, which 
directly addressed the primary reason customers cited for switching to the digital-native competitor. 
Is this approach reusable for other operators with legacy systems? Yes — the API orchestration pattern 
is broadly applicable wherever legacy system replacement is too risky to attempt in the required 
timeframe.

title: cybersecurity
question:
What are the most 
significant operational and cyber risks facing the org anization? How effectively are these risks currently 
managed, and where does ownership sit today? 
Phase 2 — Target Operating Model Design 
Cybersecurity Transformation in Omnichannel Retail 
4 
Define the future -state cybersecurity operating model, including organizational structure, reporting lines, 
decision rights, and the interface between corporate security, IT, and business units. 
Phase 3 — Strategy and Roadmap Development 
Translate the assessment into a prioritized, sequenced roadmap of initiatives across a 12 -month horizon, 
aligned to risk severity, regulatory exposure, and resource availability. 
Phase 4 — Control Design and Playbook Development 
Build the control frameworks, incident response playbooks, and technical standards required to close 
identified gaps, including identity and access management, vendor risk, and detection and response 
capability. 
Phase 5 — Pilot and Phased Rollout 
Implement priority initiatives in a controlled sequence, beginning with the highest -severity gaps and the 
business units most exposed to regulatory or reputational risk. 
Phase 6 — Embed, Monitor, and Mature 
Institutionalize governance forums, metrics, and continuous monitoring so risk management becomes a 
standing operational discipline rather than a one-time project. 
3. Key Considerations 
Several considerations shaped how the engagement was scoped and sequenced: 
• Speed versus rigor: the business was under pressure to keep expanding, so the roadmap had to 
demonstrate quick wins within 90 days without appearing to slow growth. 
• M&A integration debt: each acquired entity brought its own systems, vendors, and risk posture, 
requiring a standardized due-diligence and integration checklist for future deals. 
• Customer trust and brand exposure: a retailer's cybersecurity posture is closely tied to customer-facing 
trust; incidents involving payment data or personal information carry outsized reputational risk relative 
to their technical severity. 
• Resource constraints: the existing security team of six was sized for the pre -expansion business and

• Percentage of critical/high vulnerabilities remediated within SLA 
• Mean time to detect and mean time to contain, tracked monthly 
• Percentage of third-party vendors with a current risk assessment on file 
• Number of privileged accounts without MFA enforced 
• Security review completion rate for new product and vendor launches prior to go-live 
• Employee phishing simulation click-through rate, tracked quarterly 
Each metric was assigned an owner and a target threshold, and the full set was consolidated into a single -
page dashboard reviewed monthly by the steering committee, replacing the prior practice of ad hoc, 
incident-triggered reporting to the board. 
16. Governance Structure and Operating Model 
The target -state operating model clarified decision rights that had previously been ambiguous across 
corporate IT, the digital/e-commerce team, and the individual business units inherited through acquisition. 
• Cybersecurity Steering Committee: COO (chair), CISO, CFO, Chief Digital Officer, General Counsel — 
meets monthly, owns risk appetite and cross-functional prioritization. 
• CISO Office: owns the risk register, incident response, vendor risk program, and reports directly to the 
COO. 
• Security Champions Network: one representative per product/engineering team, reporting dotted-line 
to the CISO Office for early risk surfacing.

Committee of the board, separate from the CISO's own reporting line.

addressing the earlier instance of a control being marked complete without actually being deployed.

A few additional factors influenced the engagement's design and are worth noting for similar

• Seasonality: retail's concentration of revenue and traffic around major shopping events (e.g., Black 
Friday) meant that any control rollout affecting the checkout flow had to be scheduled and tested well

rules.

effort.

posture to a governed, measurable program integrated into how the business made expansion decisions.
